extracted.intended_audience: physicians, asylum superintendents, social scientists, and educated general readers interested in mental health and social causes of insanity
extracted.subtask_description: An analytical popular‑science essay identifying and discussing social, economic, occupational, moral, hereditary, and psychological factors believed to cause or protect against insanity in modern (19th‑century) society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilization versus savagery in insanity rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Civilized communities show higher numbers of insane persons than 'savages' because civilization both evolves delicate mental life (more easily injured) and produces strata of squalid, drunken, and sensual conditions worse than savagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation includes that educated/occupied minds are fortified against some causes, yet a mixed civilized environment (recklessness, drunkenness, poverty) produces many incurable lunatics in pauper asylums; counterpoint: some 'savages' lack these insanity‑producing causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intemperance (alcohol) as a principal cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Intemperance unmistakably leads the causes of asylum admissions; significant percentages of asylum cases are attributed to drink.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistics cited: Wilts County and Birmingham asylum data (e.g., 14% of 3,800 pauper patients in Birmingham attributed to drink, with large associated costs); alcohol's role may also underlie cases attributed to dyspepsia or overwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic trouble/domestic misery
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic trouble is a leading cause of insanity immediately following intemperance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic distress often interrelates with poverty and intemperance and is listed among top causes in asylum admission reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty and malnutrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Poverty is a major contributory cause of mental disorder, both directly and via malnutrition and poor living conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include pauper asylum populations, poor diet of factory children (lack of milk, excessive tea/coffee), and transmission of debility to offspring leading to idiocy or weak-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban vs rural differences (fresh vs persistent cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Urban districts show higher proportions of fresh, active, and transitory forms of mental disorder and greater admission rates; rural districts may show higher persistent pauper lunacy due to accumulation and migration patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lunacy Commissioners' Scottish report: more fresh pauper cases appear on poor-rolls in urban areas; rural persistence attributed to migration of the strong to cities leaving congenital idiots/chronics behind; availability of asylum accommodation and wealth affect admission rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational patterns in asylum populations
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain occupations are disproportionately represented among asylum inmates (e.g., farm-labourers and their families in county asylums; mechanics, artisans, domestic servants, clerks in borough asylums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asylum annual reports show occupation lists; occupations reflect local economy (agricultural vs manufacturing) and associated social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic shocks and disposable income (e.g., strikes) affect admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Periods with less disposable income (e.g., during prolonged strikes) show reductions in admissions attributable to decreased spending on drink and debauchery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Yellowlees' Glamorgan observation: during a nine-month strike male admissions fell by half, attributed to no money to spend on drink; implication that economic conditions influence incidence tied to consumption behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child diet and early-life nutrition in industrial families
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor diets among factory‑operatives' children (e.g., lack of milk, frequent tea/coffee) produce debility and stunted development that predispose to later mental degeneration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Fergusson's evidence from Bolton; poor feeding practices transmitted by parents who smoke/drink; comparisons of children's weights in factory vs agricultural districts support physical and nervous-system damage pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tobacco use among adolescents
rubrics_metrics.description: Early smoking or chewing tobacco (common among 12–20-year-old mill boys) is prejudicial to healthy nervous development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed as one contributing behavioral cause to poor physical and nervous system development in working-class youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime, weak-mindedness, and prison populations
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an intimate relation between criminality and mental deficiency; a notable proportion of convict populations are mentally deficient, insane, or epileptic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys/examinations of convicts and prison surgeons' reports indicate high proportions (e.g., 1 in 25 males in English convict-prisons; 12% reported in a Scottish prison population sample) suggesting hereditary or upbringing-related deficits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overwork, over-study, and business worry
rubrics_metrics.description: Severe or prolonged mental labor, over-study, and business-related anxiety can precipitate nervous breakdowns and insanity, particularly among the upper and middle classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data from private institutions (e.g., Ticehurst: admissions attributed to over-study and over-business); contextual factors (anxiety, sleep loss, dyspepsia, money troubles) often co-occur and amplify risk; examples include students, professionals, and businesspeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of occupation / idleness / monotonous luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: Underwork, a dreary monotony of life, luxury, and idle existence can produce hysteria and mental deterioration leading to insanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited of young women without useful occupation becoming morbidly sensitive; remedy recommended is useful work and occupation rather than more refinement or rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonous or repetitive occupations
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotonous continuous work (e.g., letter-sorting, shorthand writing, continuous railway traveling) has an unfavorable influence on mental health compared to diversified hard work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported admissions attributed to monotony; diversity of tasks is protective; specific employments listed among affected (architect, surveyor, accountant, schoolmaster, policeman, boot-maker, clerks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational overpressure and 'cramming' in youth
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive cramming and an over-extended curriculum in schools and examinations can injure young brains, contributing to nervous complaints, epileptic fits, prostration, and even suicide among exam candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cases of girls harmed by cramming; concerns about University of London's preliminary examinations and medical degree standards; warnings against forcing feeble, ill-fed children into heavy study; examiners deplore multiplicity of subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary predisposition / constitutional weakness
rubrics_metrics.description: Many insane persons show long-standing peculiarities or latent constitutional tendencies; heredity and being 'never wholly whole-minded' predispose to later attacks when stressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On careful inquiry a smouldering constitutional susceptibility is often found preceding an episode; child-rearing in civilization can allow weak constitutions to survive and manifest as imbecility or later insanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/psychical causes (religious excitement, fanaticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral and psychical agents—religious excitement, waves of religious fervor, and extreme utterances by leaders—can upset mental equilibrium and produce delusions or mass cases of insanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious excitement considered more significant than spiritualism; responsibility of orators/leaders warned; spiritualism is mentioned as less important but previously exaggerated in some claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class‑specific causal patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Different social classes have different predominant causes: among the poor, beer/gin, malnutrition, monotony, and poverty; among the middle classes, business stress, competition, failures, and intemperance; among the upper classes, intemperance and over-refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay emphasizes that causes vary by class and that both extremes (excessive activity and excessive dullness) can lead to the same result; policy implication: class-sensitive preventive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological narrowness, isolation, and doctrinal prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: A restricted area of psychical activity (from narrow parental training, ecclesiastical influences, or solitary life) leads the mind to brood on trivialities, develop delusions, religious scruples, or morbid suspicions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such persons may avoid vices yet become asylum inmates due to hyper‑sensitivity and inability to cope with novel assertions; social and intellectual breadth is protective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction and multifactorial causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Insanity usually arises from multiple interacting causes rather than a single factor; factors like alcohol, poverty, heredity, overwork, and anxiety often combine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors caution against simple attribution (e.g., to overwork alone) and stress the need to consider concomitants (sleeplessness, vice, worry). Statistical ratios (accumulated pauper lunacy vs fresh cases) are of limited use without minute investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventability and remedy through social improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A considerable portion of lunacy is preventable by improving moral and physical conditions: reducing intemperance, improving nutrition, providing useful occupation, moderating educational demands, and addressing poverty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclusion urges social reform (improving conditions of squalid classes, education and training to fortify minds) and targeted remedies (work rather than rest for some women; diversification of employment tasks).
